source.title: Platonic Representations in the Human Brain: Unsupervised Recovery of Universal Geometry
source.authors: Pablo Marcos-Manchón; Rishi Jha; L. Fuentemilla

record.tranche_reason: The study tests a biological extension of the Platonic representation idea: it measures whether independently learned human brain-response spaces can be aligned across subjects, and compares brain-to-brain with model-to-brain alignment. It does not test convergence among AI models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports cross-subject brain-space translation and model-to-brain alignment results. These concern human neural representations, not convergence between AI models or vision-language models. Within-subject encoder results and cited prior-work results are not recorded as rows because they do not measure cross-system convergence.
record.test_reason: The study adapts the strong-PRH unpaired translation method (mini-vec2vec) to human fMRI. It reports brain-to-brain and brain-to-model mapping performance. None of V1–V7 concerns human brains: they name convergence among artificial networks. No experiment maps one AI model onto another or varies model scale to measure model-model alignment. The rows therefore bear on no version; the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that independently learned fMRI embedding spaces are approximately isometric across subjects and translatable by unsupervised orthogonal rotations, and that synchronization improves retrieval. They also conclude that tested model spaces predict neural embeddings but are not related to them by the same near-isometric transforms.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts mini-vec2vec-style unsupervised orthogonal translation to independently learned fMRI embeddings, with repeated-presentation self-supervision and evaluation on held-out shared images. The paper tests human brain spaces rather than AI-model convergence.
record.method_sensitivity: Pairwise translation is sensitive to initialization; the main results select the best-performing of 10 random seeds per ordered subject pair. Averaging the 10 rotations and projecting back to O(d) gives Mean Rank 4.61 ± 4.37, versus 2.56 ± 1.71 for best-seed results (Appendix C.2, Figure S3).

fits_no_version.finding: Independently learned subject-specific fMRI embeddings are translated across 8 subjects by unsupervised orthogonal rotations. Mean Rank is 2.56 and R@1 0.78 (chance 258 and 0.002). Synchronizing into one shared space improves this to Mean Rank 1.97 and R@1 0.83. Without seed selection, Mean Rank is 4.61 ± 4.37.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human visual-cortex representations are approximately isometric across individuals and can be aligned without paired data (a biological analogue of the strong PRH).

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised maps from pretrained model spaces to brain embeddings give weaker retrieval than brain-to-brain translation, especially under semi-orthogonal maps. The best semi-orthogonal result is Mean Rank 13.33 and R@1 0.29; ridge does better.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model and brain representational spaces share stimulus information but are not related by near-isometric transforms.

fits_no_version.finding: Table S4 reports brain-to-model ridge retrieval by model size, within subjects. The trend is mixed: larger DINOv2 models map worse (Mean Rank 24.82 for S rising to 42.31 for G), while larger AugReg ViTs map slightly better (25.27 for T falling to 20.30 for L). These results are not recorded as rows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Brain–model alignment does not consistently increase with model scale.

record.problems: The evidence is for human fMRI subjects, not convergence among AI models. Evaluation uses 515 held-out shared images and high-quality data with repeated stimulus presentations. The pairwise procedure is initialization-sensitive, and the main results use the best of 10 seeds per pair. Some figure-level pairwise results are not transcribed individually here.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 and Figure 3 show individual ordered subject-pair values; these were not transcribed cell by cell. Appendix C.2 Figure S3 reports per-pair seed comparisons and a distribution of seed-candidate outcomes, also omitted. Within-subject encoder results (Sections 4.1 and Appendix B/C) do not measure cross-system convergence. Table 3's flattened layout makes the association of its two Entropic GW results with representation rows less clear than the main result; the entries above preserve that ambiguity in the notes.

untested.parts: All of it: no AI model-to-model alignment is measured as a function of scale or capability.
All of it: no vision–language model alignment on paired data.
All of it: no networks trained from different seeds are compared.
All of it for AI models. Only brain-to-brain and model-to-brain maps are fitted; no model-to-model map.
All of it: no feature- or circuit-level comparison across models.
All of it for AI models. Metric dependence appears only for brain spaces (orthogonal vs Entropic GW; semi-orthogonal vs ridge).
All of it for AI models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' was changed. The study extends the PRH idea to biological systems but measures no AI-model convergence, so no row meets the same-kind-of-system requirement for any version. The main results use best-of-10-seed selection per pair. Also unrecorded: Table 3's model-guided cross-subject baselines (ViT AugReg-L/16 + Ridge reaches Mean Rank 5.54). Like the other model–brain rows, they would bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: AI models' representations becoming more aligned with model size or capability.
Alignment between vision and language model representations of paired images and captions as model performance changes.
Feature or subspace convergence across independently initialized networks of the same architecture.
Mapping between AI model representations. The study maps human subject-specific brain embeddings to one another and maps model embeddings to brain embeddings.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Dependence of AI-model convergence on similarity metrics, metric settings, or input distribution.
Whether AI-model alignment is incomplete or explained by shared training data or objectives.
